metaDescription: Six patio heaters under $250 covering propane towers and mounted or hanging infrared units, with advice on which style suits wind, seating and wiring.
expertTake: The Hykolity 50,000 BTU table-design tower is the best overall pick for a large open deck, with the Garvee tripod infrared as the best electric alternative that needs no installation. The Sundate hanging unit is the pick for a covered pergola. Anyone with a small balcony should skip gas entirely. Decide propane or infrared first, then pick the stability and control details that suit your space. Whichever style you choose, set it up before the first cold night and test it with the people who will sit there.
introParagraphs: This is the price where the two technologies compete directly. A propane tower gives the widest warm circle on an open deck, while a mounted or tripod infrared heater gives silent, fuel-free warmth that survives a breeze.
The right choice depends on where you sit, how much wind you get and whether you can wire a heater in. The $250 cap reflects listing prices on the date this guide was updated, and prices move.

products.name: Hykolity 50,000 BTU propane patio heater, table design, button ignition
products.description:
This Hykolity is a 50,000 BTU propane tower with a stainless steel burner, button ignition that needs no battery and a table-style base that hides the tank. A triple protection system covers tip-over and flame-out behaviour, and wheels let you move it into place. It is the straightforward answer for warming a deck or patio where a group sits in a circle.

Fifty thousand BTU per hour is about ten times the output of a 1500 watt electric heater. That is what gives it a warm circle of perhaps ten to fifteen feet in calm air, far beyond any plug-in unit. In wind the circle shrinks, so place it on the windward side of the group, with a screen if possible. Compared with the infrared units, it needs fuel and clearance from overhead cover, but it has no wiring and no outlet limit.

Keep a spare cylinder because a 20 pound tank lasts roughly eight to ten hours on high. Leak-test the connections with soapy water at the start of each season, keep the dome clear of umbrellas and branches, and cover it when not in use. Assembly takes about an hour and two people. Tighten the post sections before connecting the tank, open the valve slowly and give the flame a minute to settle on low before raising it.
products.bestFor: Open decks with a group of four to eight.
pros: 50,000 BTU output with a wide warm circle
Tank hidden in a table-style base

products.name: Garvee 1500W infrared freestanding patio heater with tripod
products.description:
The Garvee is a carbon fiber infrared heater on a tripod stand, with three power steps at 500, 1000 and 1500 watts, a remote and a 24 hour timer. The aluminum body is designed for outdoor patios. As a plug-in freestanding unit it needs no wiring, which makes it the easy electric choice.

Infrared warms people and objects directly rather than the air, so wind matters less than for a fan heater or a propane tower. Output is capped at 1500 watts, about 5,100 BTU, and effective for a seating group of perhaps 100 to 150 square feet. Compared with the Hykolity propane tower, it has far less reach but no fuel, no flame and no fumes.

Place it close to the seating and aimed slightly down. Use a weather-protected outlet and check the plug after the first hour. In practice, set the Garvee a metre or two from the seats at chest height and let it run on the middle step; the top step is rarely needed once everyone is warm. A tripod can wobble on soft ground, so place it on pavers and check each leg is firm before you walk away.
products.bestFor: A plug-in heater for a small seating group.
cons: Glow element is hot to touch

products.name: Sundate hanging WiFi patio heater, 1500W, 9 heat levels
products.description:
The Sundate is a hanging carbon fiber infrared heater with nine heat levels, a 24 hour timer and control by WiFi app, remote or touch panel. The listing cites 95 percent thermal efficiency, which for a resistance heater is plausible because nearly all the electricity becomes heat. Hanging it overhead keeps the floor clear.

The tradeoff is installation. A ceiling or beam mount needs a secure fixing and a power connection, so it suits a covered pergola or a porch more than a table-top setup. Compared with the Garvee, it is neater and smarter but less flexible.

WiFi control is a convenience, not a necessity. Keep manual or remote control as a backup. If you pick a smart heater, make sure you can still operate it without the app when the router is down. Mounting height and cable routing matter more than app features, so plan the install with the manual in hand before you buy.

products.name: SPECRAFT 1500W carbon fiber infrared heater, wall or ceiling mount
products.description:
The SPECRAFT is a carbon fiber infrared heater with a quartz tube, three heat levels, a remote and a 24 hour timer. It can be mounted on a wall or hung from a ceiling. It is a simple, direct infrared bar.

It competes with the Sundate but is simpler, with fewer levels and no WiFi. The mount is still an installation job.

Check clearance from the ceiling and keep the area below clear. Mounting is usually done by a handyperson or electrician, and the cost of that labour belongs in your budget. Confirm the mount accepts your wall or beam, and that the cable length reaches the supply without an extension.
products.bestFor: A simple wall or ceiling infrared bar.

products.name: Hykolity 50,000 BTU patio heater with sand box and conical barrel
products.description:
This Hykolity variant adds a sand box in the base and a conical barrel that the listing says is more stable. It has the same 50,000 BTU output and double-layer stainless burner. Extra weight is the cheapest stability feature.

It is the better tower for a gusty deck. The sand makes it harder to move.

Fill the sand box and keep it dry. It is the one for a deck where the wind regularly knocks over lightweight things. Move it with the sand box empty if you can, and level it before filling. Check the wheels and locks each season.

products.name: Sweetcrispy 48,000 BTU patio heater with double-layer burner
products.description:
The Sweetcrispy offers 48,000 BTU behind a double-layer 304 stainless burner and automatic shutoff. It rolls on wheels.

It is nearly identical in output to the Hykolity and stakes its claim on burner build.

Leak-test and keep clear of overhead cover. The burner is the part most owners notice in year three, so check for an even blue flame and clean the ports each season. Wipe the stainless after rain and keep a cover on it in the off-season. It rolls well on a smooth patio but struggles on gravel, so plan a permanent spot on a flat surface. Its output is nearly the same as the Hykolity, so the decision rests on how much you value the burner mesh and the price on the day. Cover it when not in use, and check the regulator and hose each season.
products.bestFor: Owners who care about burner longevity.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 50,000 BTU propane tower like the Hykolity warms a ten to fifteen foot circle, while a 1500W infrared like the Garvee warms 100 to 150 square feet. Choose propane for big open decks and infrared for small or breezy spots. For a six-seat table, a 50,000 BTU tower or two 1500W infrared heaters placed at either end are the realistic answers. A quick check before buying is to sketch your seating and mark the heater position, then measure the distance to the farthest seat.

Propane towers lose convective heat in a breeze. Infrared warms people directly, so the Garvee, Sundate and SPECRAFT hold up better. Walk your space on a windy evening before you decide. Heat from infrared falls off quickly with distance, so seat people within about two to three metres. Consider an outdoor-rated timer plug for any plug-in unit, which adds a layer of protection against leaving it on.

The Sundate and SPECRAFT mount to a wall or ceiling and need a secure fixing and power. The Garvee plugs in. The towers need nothing but a tank. Mounted heaters should sit above head height with the clearance the manual states, and nobody should be able to touch the tubes.

Propane heaters are for open air only, well clear of overhead cover, and never in a garage or enclosed porch. Infrared units need the manual's clearance as well. Check that your outlet is weather-protected and ground-fault protected before plugging in any electric unit.

The Sundate adds WiFi and nine levels. The Garvee offers three steps and a 24 hour timer. A timer is a simple safeguard against leaving a heater on. A propane tower that is perfectly safe in open air becomes dangerous under a low roof, so never move it under cover.
A tall tower is easy to knock over. The sand-box Hykolity adds weight. Mounted infrared cannot tip. Where the manual and the listing differ, follow the manual.

specDecoder.meaning: Heat output per hour. Compare BTU only within the same fuel type, since electric and propane are not comparable by watts alone.
Radiant heat that warms objects directly. It warms what is in front of it, not the air.
A set of safety shutoffs. These cut gas or power when the heater tilts or the flame dies.
Share of input turned into heat. A high figure means almost all the power becomes heat, which is true of any resistance heater.
Power steps. More levels let you run at a lower, cheaper setting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared BTU and wattage. The 50,000 BTU towers led. We read radius and coverage claims as best cases.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wind behaviour
howWeEvaluated.description: We favoured infrared in breezy spots. Installation burden was treated as a real cost for the mounted units.

howWeEvaluated.title: Installation
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted wiring and mounting as costs. Where two units were near-identical, certification and clear manuals broke the tie.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared shutoffs and clearance needs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on spec sheets and listing feedback patterns, we weighed reports of ignition trouble and weak output. We also considered how well each listing explains its mounting and clearance.

howToChoose.note: Count your seats and measure the spread, because that decides whether one heater or two will do. A realistic starting point for a mid-size deck is one tower or two infrared heaters.
Prices move, so read these tiers as relative positions.

cards.label: Propane
cards.text: The Hykolity and Sweetcrispy warm a wide circle but need fuel and open air.

cards.label: Infrared
cards.text: The Garvee, Sundate and SPECRAFT are silent and fuel-free but limited to 1500W.

howToChoose.note: Pick propane for open decks; infrared for covered, small or breezy spots. If your patio is large, think about two infrared heaters at opposite ends rather than a single tower in the middle.
Installation can change the real cost, so budget for it. Wiring rules differ by region, so check local requirements before buying a mounted unit.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A mounted infrared with clearance, never a propane tower under cover.

howToChoose.note: A pergola with a solid roof rules out propane.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You host large groups. Two towers beat one.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You warm a bench. The SPECRAFT is enough.

howToChoose.note: A tower costs more to run per hour than an infrared unit, so factor fuel into the choice if you use it nightly.

maintenance.why: Gas leaks are the most serious risk. Skipping this is how small leaks go unnoticed for a whole season, so use soapy water and look for bubbles.
Debris cuts output. A dirty reflector or burner reduces output noticeably.
Loose brackets and frayed cords are hazards. A frayed cord or a loose bracket should be fixed before the next use.
Sand or water keeps a tower stable. A tower that has lost ballast is the one that tips.
Rain damages igniters and electronics. A cover and dry spot extend igniter and electronics life.

faq.a: Propane for open decks, electric infrared for covered or small spaces.

faq.q: How long does a tank last?
faq.a: Roughly eight to ten hours on high. Many owners end up with a tower for parties and a small infrared unit for everyday evenings.

faq.q: Can I use propane under a pergola?
faq.a: Not under solid cover unless the manual allows it. A licensed electrician is the safe route for anything hardwired.
Better than fan heaters and propane towers. Propane smells like rotten eggs when it leaks, so shut the valve and move away if you notice it.
For hardwired mounted units, yes. Remember that mounted heaters need an outlet or junction within reach of the cable.

faq.q: How many heaters do I need?
faq.a: One per seating group. Cover the tower or bring electric units inside to extend their life. If you are unsure, start with one heater and add a second only if people at the edges are cold. Pairing a tower with a small infrared unit covers both the party and the quiet evening.
